objectives.text: The learner can derive the formula from the product rule
The learner can choose u and dv so the integral gets simpler
The learner can recognise when to apply it twice

steps.note: twice, for x squared e to the x

say: Integration by parts is not a new idea. It is the product rule, read backwards. Let me show you where it comes from, because if you can rebuild it you will never misremember it.

board.text: Start from something you already know.

say: Now integrate both sides. On the left, integrating a derivative just gives back what you started with. Rearrange, and there it is.

board.text: You are trading one integral for another. It only helps if the new one is easier.

say: Watch it work. I want the integral of x times cosine x. I will call x the u, because differentiating it makes it simpler, and cosine x d x the d v, because I can integrate that easily.
Now let me show you the other choice, because seeing it fail is worth more than being told to avoid it. Suppose I picked u equals cosine x instead.

board.text: The same integral, with the choices swapped.
x squared — going the wrong way
Pick u so that differentiating it simplifies things.

say: Sometimes once is not enough. For x squared times e to the x, one round leaves you with x times e to the x, which is still a product. So you do it again.

board.text: Each pass drops the power by one. A polynomial of degree n takes n passes.

say: One habit worth carrying: when you are choosing u, go down this list and take the first type that appears. Logarithms, then inverse trig, then algebraic, then trig, then exponential.

board.text: It is a habit, not a law. The test is always: did the new integral get simpler?

summary: We built integration by parts out of the product rule, used it on x cos x, saw what a bad choice of u costs, and applied it twice for x squared e to the x.
